source_cards.front: What extra rule applies to remote-path practice hours for a motorcycle license?
source_cards.back: For a motorcycle license on the remote path, all one hundred practice hours must be driven in daylight only.

source_cards.front: How does supervision differ for a Class C permit and a motorcycle permit?
source_cards.back: A Class C permit supervisor sits in the seat beside you, while a motorcycle or moped permit supervisor must ride a motorcycle within direct sight and may not be in a car or truck.

source_cards.front: What limits apply to a motorcycle or moped permit holder?
source_cards.back: A Class M or M-Z permit holder rides in daylight only, carries no passengers and stays off limited-access highways and freeways.

source_cards.front: What do Classes A, B and M cover?
source_cards.back: Class A covers combinations rated over twenty-six thousand pounds GCWR with a trailer over ten thousand pounds, Class B covers a single vehicle over twenty-six thousand pounds GVWR that may tow under ten thousand pounds, and Class M covers motorcycles and mopeds.

source_cards.front: How long does a motorcycle permit last at different ages?
source_cards.back: A motorcycle permit issued between fifteen and a half and eighteen lasts one year, but one issued after age seventeen expires on the eighteenth birthday; at eighteen or older it lasts six months and can be renewed only once every five years.

source_cards.front: What vehicles does Class C cover, and what may it tow?

source_cards.front: What does the J endorsement allow a Class C driver to tow, and within what limits?
source_cards.back: The J endorsement lets a Class C driver tow a vehicle or combination rated above ten thousand pounds, provided the combination stays within seventy feet and twenty-six thousand pounds; above twenty-six thousand pounds a Class A license is required.

source_cards.front: How does Nevada describe seat belts, and are they optional?
source_cards.back: Nevada calls seat belts your best protection against injury or death in a crash, and wearing them is required by law, not just advised.

source_cards.front: What share of Nevada highway deaths were unbelted drivers in the year the handbook cites?
source_cards.back: In two thousand twenty, drivers who were not wearing seat belts made up twenty-three point zero three percent of Nevada highway fatalities, an increase of one point one five percent over two thousand sixteen.

source_cards.front: Which seat belts must a car of model year nineteen sixty-eight or newer have?
source_cards.back: A car of model year nineteen sixty-eight or newer must have lap-type seat belts for the front-seat passengers.

source_cards.front: Which seat belts must a car of model year nineteen seventy or newer have?
source_cards.back: A car of model year nineteen seventy or newer must have lap-type belts for every passenger plus shoulder harnesses for the front seat.

source_cards.front: How do the nineteen sixty-eight and nineteen seventy seat belt rules differ?
source_cards.back: Model year nineteen sixty-eight brought lap belts for front-seat passengers, while model year nineteen seventy brought lap belts for every passenger and front-seat shoulder harnesses.

source_cards.front: Who must wear a safety belt when the vehicle has one?
source_cards.back: The driver and every passenger aged six or older must wear a safety belt whenever the vehicle has one.

source_cards.front: Which children must ride in an approved child restraint system?
source_cards.back: Children under six, and children shorter than fifty-seven inches, must ride in an approved child restraint system (NRS 484B point one five seven).

source_cards.front: How can the child restraint law affect the driver's own license?
source_cards.back: For children, the restraint law reaches the driver's license itself, since failing to restrain a young child can bring a license suspension as well as fines or community service.

source_cards.front: How must a child under two ride?
source_cards.back: A child under two must ride in a rear-facing child restraint system in the back seat.

source_cards.front: What two child-seating practices must you never use?
source_cards.back: Never hold a child on your lap or share one safety belt between a child and another person.

source_cards.front: What do age two, age six and the height rule each mark for child passengers?
source_cards.back: Age two marks the rear-facing back-seat rule, age six marks both the start of the adult belt requirement and the end of the under-six restraint rule, though a child still under fifty-seven inches keeps needing a restraint.

source_cards.front: What do booster seats and belt-positioning seats do?
source_cards.back: Booster seats and belt-positioning seats raise or position a child so the vehicle's seat belt can secure the child safely.

source_cards.front: What two things should you check about a child restraint before travelling?
source_cards.back: Before travelling with a child, check that the restraint is approved by the US Department of Transportation under the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and suits the child's size and weight.

source_cards.front: How must a child restraint be installed?
source_cards.back: A child restraint must be installed safely and securely, following the manufacturer's instructions or another method approved by NHTSA.

source_cards.front: Which way do infants always face, and why?
source_cards.back: Infants are always buckled in facing the rear, because a rear-facing seat supports the baby's head and shields the neck and spine in most crashes.

source_cards.front: How does a booster seat differ from a rear-facing infant seat?
source_cards.back: A booster or belt-positioning seat works with the vehicle's own seat belt, while a rear-facing seat holds the infant itself and protects the head, neck and spine.

source_cards.front: How do you keep a child's head away from an inflating airbag?
source_cards.back: To keep a child's head away from an inflating airbag, use a restraint with a full harness or a properly fitted shoulder and lap belt.

source_cards.front: What should you check once the engine is running and before you move?
source_cards.back: Once the engine runs, check the fuel gauge and warning lights, keep the stereo low enough to hear traffic, switch on headlights, signal or wipers if needed, and before moving stop, look and listen for traffic, cyclists and pedestrians.

source_cards.front: What does a green arrow allow, and whom must you still yield to?
source_cards.back: A green arrow lets you go the way it points and protects the turn from other traffic, yet you must still yield to pedestrians, bicycles and vehicles already in the intersection.

source_cards.front: What do the octagon, diamond, rectangle and inverted triangle shapes mean?
source_cards.back: Sign shapes: an eight-sided octagon means stop, a diamond means warning, a rectangle gives regulations or directions, and an inverted triangle means yield right-of-way.

source_cards.front: Where do you stop when there is no stop line or crosswalk?
source_cards.back: Where no stop line or crosswalk exists, slow and stop if needed at the point closest to the intersection that gives a view of oncoming through traffic, then yield to pedestrians and cross traffic before going.

source_cards.front: Who goes first at a four-way stop?
source_cards.back: At a four-way stop, wait for vehicles already in the intersection and let vehicles that arrived before you go first.

source_cards.front: How does a yield sign differ in practice from a stop sign, and whom must you yield to?
source_cards.back: A yield sign works like a stop sign except you may keep moving without a full stop when it is safe; slow down and yield to pedestrians, through traffic, drivers already on the highway and vehicles making a U-turn.

source_cards.front: What must you do when an emergency vehicle approaches with siren and red lights?
source_cards.back: When a police car, fire engine, ambulance or other emergency vehicle approaches with its siren and red lights on, pull to the right edge and stop until it has passed, but never stop inside an intersection.

source_cards.front: What must you do when traffic lights are out?
source_cards.back: When traffic lights are out, come to a full stop, yield to pedestrians and to vehicles already stopped or in the intersection, then proceed with caution.

source_cards.front: Where must you stop at a red light, and for how long?
source_cards.back: At a red light, stop completely behind the crosswalk or stop line, or before entering the intersection if neither exists, and stay stopped until the light turns green.

source_cards.front: What does a steady yellow light mean?
source_cards.back: A steady yellow light warns that red is coming: stop if you have not entered the intersection, keep going and clear it if you already have, and never speed up to beat the light.

source_cards.front: What do flashing red and flashing yellow lights mean?
source_cards.back: A flashing red light means a full stop and going only when the road is clear and you have the right-of-way, exactly like a stop sign, while a flashing yellow light means proceed with caution.

source_cards.front: What do a steady yellow arrow and a flashing yellow arrow mean?
source_cards.back: A steady yellow arrow warns that the arrow is about to turn red and you should clear the intersection; a flashing yellow arrow lets you turn after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.

source_cards.front: What does a green arrow allow, and whom must you still yield to?
source_cards.back: A green arrow lets you go the way it points and protects the turn from other traffic, yet you must still yield to pedestrians, bicycles and vehicles already in the intersection.

source_cards.front: How do the steady yellow light, flashing yellow light and flashing yellow arrow differ?
source_cards.back: A steady yellow light means stop if you can before entering, a flashing yellow light means go ahead with caution, and a flashing yellow arrow means turn only after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.

source_cards.front: How must pedestrians follow red, yellow and green traffic lights?
source_cards.back: Pedestrians at intersections must obey traffic signals: on red they do not cross, on yellow they must not start across, and on green they may cross, unless a pedestrian signal or officer directs otherwise.

source_cards.front: What does a lit WALK signal mean for pedestrians and drivers?
source_cards.back: A lit WALK sign or walking-person symbol lets pedestrians cross in the signal's direction, and the drivers of all vehicles must give them the right-of-way.

source_cards.front: Where do most pedestrian deaths happen, and who is responsible?
source_cards.back: Most pedestrian deaths happen mid-block, between intersections, and both drivers and pedestrians share responsibility, so drivers should always be ready to yield.

source_cards.front: Where must you stop and yield for pedestrians at crosswalks?
source_cards.back: Always stop before a crosswalk, and at intersections where no crosswalk is painted you must still yield to pedestrians.

source_cards.front: What are stop lines and dotted white lines for?
source_cards.back: Stop lines are wide white lines across a lane where you stop with a view of traffic from every direction, and dotted white lines either carry a lane line through an intersection or mark freeway exit-only lanes.

source_cards.front: Why must drivers always yield to trains?
source_cards.back: A train cannot stop in time to avoid a car, its speed is hard to judge, and a crossbuck means drivers must yield to trains.

source_cards.front: What colors are pavement markings, and what do broken white lines mean?
source_cards.back: Pavement markings are white or yellow, and broken white lines divide lanes moving the same way; stay inside your lane without straddling, and pass only when safe.

source_cards.front: What does a solid white line mean?
source_cards.back: A solid white line between same-direction lanes means no lane changes and no passing, and solid white also marks the highway edge and the line between a travel lane and the shoulder.

source_cards.front: What do broken and solid yellow lines mean?
source_cards.back: Yellow lines divide traffic moving in opposite directions: a broken yellow line allows passing when safe, while a solid yellow line means do not cross or pass and also marks the left edge of multi-lane divided highways.

source_cards.front: When may you not pass with double yellow lines?
source_cards.back: With double yellow lines, you may not pass if the line on your side is solid.

source_cards.front: What may a center left-turn lane be used for?
source_cards.back: A center left-turn lane, edged by solid and broken yellow lines, may be crossed only to turn left onto or off the highway and is never a travel or passing lane.

source_cards.front: How do broken white and solid white lane lines differ?
source_cards.back: Broken white separates same-direction lanes and allows passing when safe, while solid white between same-direction lanes forbids lane changes and passing.

source_cards.back: Sign shapes: a pennant means no passing, a five-sided pentagon marks school zones and crossings, a circle warns of a railroad crossing ahead, a crossbuck marks the crossing itself and a shield is a route marker.

source_cards.back: Railroad crossing signs warn you to slow and possibly stop; look both ways and stay off the tracks whenever a train is approaching.

source_cards.back: At a railroad crossing with a stop sign you must stop, and when a train is coming you must stop at least fifteen feet from the tracks.

source_cards.back: Passenger buses and trucks hauling flammable or dangerous materials must stop at railroad crossings even when no signal shows and no train is coming.

source_cards.front: How do the stopping and parking distances at railroad tracks differ?
source_cards.back: Stop at least fifteen feet from the tracks when a train comes, but never park within fifty feet of the nearest rail.

source_cards.front: What two speed limits can a school zone have, and how do lights help?
source_cards.back: School-zone limits are either fifteen or twenty-five miles per hour, and some zones use flashing yellow lights to show when the lower limit is in effect.

source_cards.front: How does a yield sign differ in practice from a stop sign, and whom must you yield to?
source_cards.back: A yield sign works like a stop sign except you may keep moving without a full stop when it is safe; slow down and yield to pedestrians, through traffic, drivers already on the highway and vehicles making a U-turn.

source_cards.front: When may you turn right on a red light?
source_cards.back: Unless a sign prohibits it, you may turn right on red after a complete stop, signalling first and waiting until vehicles and pedestrians are clear.

source_cards.front: What does a green light allow?
source_cards.back: A green light allows going straight, turning right or turning left unless a sign forbids the turn.

source_cards.front: When is a left turn on red allowed?
source_cards.back: A left turn on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street whose traffic flows to the left, after signalling, stopping fully and yielding, unless a sign, arrow or officer forbids it.

source_cards.front: When are U-turns allowed in a school zone?
source_cards.back: U-turns in a school zone are banned except when no children are present, on days without school, outside the half-hour windows around the school day, or when signs or lights show the zone is not in effect.

source_cards.front: What may a center left-turn lane be used for?
source_cards.back: A center left-turn lane, edged by solid and broken yellow lines, may be crossed only to turn left onto or off the highway and is never a travel or passing lane.

source_cards.front: How far may you drive in a center turn lane before and after a left turn?
source_cards.back: You may drive no more than two hundred feet in a center turn lane before turning left, and no more than fifty feet in it after turning onto the highway before merging (NRS 484B point two two three).

source_cards.front: Does Nevada law give anyone the right-of-way?
source_cards.back: Nevada law does not hand anyone the right-of-way; it only says who has to yield, and even a driver who legally may go first must do everything possible to avoid a crash.

source_cards.front: At an intersection with no signs or signals, who usually goes first?
source_cards.back: At an intersection with no signs or signals, the vehicle on your right should usually go first.

source_cards.front: Who goes first: a vehicle already in the intersection or one just arriving?
source_cards.back: A vehicle that is already in the intersection goes before vehicles that are only now arriving.

source_cards.front: Who has priority: a straight-through vehicle in the intersection or a left-turning one?
source_cards.back: A vehicle going straight that is already in the intersection has priority over a vehicle turning left; the left-turner may go once it has yielded and signalled.

source_cards.front: Whom must you yield to when entering a main road from a driveway?
source_cards.back: Drivers coming onto a main road from a minor road, a private road or a driveway must yield to all traffic on the main road and to pedestrians.

source_cards.front: Which two drivers must yield in the intersection and driveway rules?
source_cards.back: A left-turning driver yields to straight-through traffic already in the intersection, and a driver leaving a driveway or private road yields to everything on the main road, pedestrians included.

source_cards.front: What must you do when an emergency vehicle approaches with siren or flashing lights?
source_cards.back: When an emergency vehicle using its siren or flashing lights approaches from any direction, pull over at once to the right edge, staying out of any intersection, and wait stopped until it goes by.

source_cards.front: Who goes first at a four-way stop?
source_cards.back: At a four-way stop, the driver who reached the intersection first goes first, after a complete stop.

source_cards.front: How does the right-of-way order differ at an uncontrolled intersection and a four-way stop?
source_cards.back: At an uncontrolled intersection the vehicle on the right usually goes first, but at a four-way stop the order is set by who arrived and stopped first.

source_cards.front: Whom do you yield to when joining a freeway?
source_cards.back: When joining a freeway, yield to the traffic already on it and enter only when it is safe.

source_cards.front: Must you yield to bicyclists in a bike lane or on a bike path?
source_cards.back: Yield to bicyclists riding in a bike lane or on a bike path.

source_cards.front: How must you treat a funeral procession?
source_cards.back: Yield to a funeral procession and let the vehicles with their headlights on pass together as one group.

source_cards.front: Who has the right-of-way at crosswalks and intersections, and what should pedestrians still check?
source_cards.back: Vehicles must give way to pedestrians in crosswalks and at intersections, yet before stepping off the curb they should make sure cars in both directions have stopped.

source_cards.front: What must drivers do for a blind pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog?
source_cards.back: A blind or visually impaired person on foot who uses a guide dog or other service animal, or carries a white cane or walking stick, has the right-of-way; drivers must yield, stop fully if needed and take care before going on (NRS 484B point two nine zero).

source_cards.front: Why are freeways usually the safest roads?
source_cards.back: Freeways are usually the safest roads because access is limited, traffic flows one way without stopping, and drivers meet no intersections, signals, railroad crossings or sharp curves.

source_cards.front: How do the duties of merging drivers and drivers already on the freeway differ?
source_cards.back: Merging drivers must yield to traffic already on the freeway, while drivers already on it should watch for merging cars and adjust speed so merges stay smooth.

source_cards.front: What do you do at a ramp meter that is switched on?
source_cards.back: When a ramp meter is switched on, pull up to the stop line and stop on red, expect it to change faster than an intersection signal, wait for green, then follow the ramp and merge safely.

source_cards.front: Where should you slow down when leaving a freeway?

source_cards.front: What does stopping distance depend on?
source_cards.back: Stopping distance depends on vehicle type and weight, speed, tire and brake condition, road surface, reaction time, alertness or fatigue, and the weather.

source_cards.front: How does braking time differ from braking distance?
source_cards.back: Braking time is how long the brakes and tire-road friction need to stop the vehicle, while braking distance is how far it travels during that time.

source_cards.front: What happens to braking distance when you double your speed?
source_cards.back: Doubling your speed, for example from thirty miles per hour to sixty miles per hour, makes the braking distance four times as long, not twice as long.

source_cards.front: How do wet roads and the first rain of a season affect stopping?
source_cards.back: On a wet road stopping distance can be more than double the dry figure, and the first rain of a season is especially dangerous because oil mixes with water on the pavement.

source_cards.front: How long is the stopping distance on ice at thirty miles per hour?
source_cards.back: At thirty miles per hour on ice the stopping distance would be three hundred seventy-three feet, more than the length of a football field.

source_cards.front: In the stopping table, how far does a car take to stop from forty-five miles per hour?
source_cards.back: In the same table, stopping from forty-five miles per hour takes about two hundred seventy-eight feet in all, made up of one hundred sixty-five feet of perception and reaction distance and one hundred thirteen feet of braking distance.

source_cards.front: Why do turns need extra care, and what should you do before and after turning?
source_cards.back: Many crashes come from drivers making turns, so watch for pedestrians and bicyclists, look once more in each direction before turning, and cancel the signal after joining traffic.

source_cards.front: How must you pass a bicyclist?
source_cards.back: To pass a cyclist, move into the next lane to the left if there is one going your way and it is reasonably safe; otherwise pass at a safe distance of at least three feet and do not move back right until clear.

source_cards.front: May you drive in a marked bicycle lane?

source_cards.front: What should you do when you park and leave the vehicle?
source_cards.back: When you park and leave the vehicle, turn off the engine and set the parking brake, and look for bicycles and other vehicles before opening your door.

source_cards.front: Whom do you yield to when entering a roundabout, and which way does traffic go?
source_cards.back: Drivers entering a roundabout must yield to the traffic already circulating in it, and all traffic travels around it counterclockwise.

source_cards.front: Where must pedestrians cross at a roundabout?
source_cards.back: Pedestrians at a roundabout must stay in the marked crosswalks and never cross to the central island; they have the right-of-way but should still watch for cars.

source_cards.front: Which lane do you enter after a right turn, and when may you change lanes?
source_cards.back: After a right turn, enter the right-hand lane of the new road or the lane marked for the turn, and change lanes only after signalling once you are well clear of the intersection.

source_cards.front: What steps make a lane change safe?
source_cards.back: To change lanes, check the rear and side mirrors, signal at least one hundred feet ahead in the city or three hundred feet on highways and freeways, look over your shoulder at the blind spot, and never change lanes inside an intersection.

source_cards.front: Where is a U-turn legal?
source_cards.back: A U-turn is legal across a double yellow line when safe and legal, at an intersection on a green light or green arrow unless a No U-turn sign is posted, and on a divided highway only through an opening in the divider.

source_cards.front: Why can't you make a U-turn mid-block in a business district?
source_cards.back: Never make a U-turn in a business district, which also covers areas with churches, apartments, multifamily housing and public buildings; there, turn only at an intersection or a provided opening.

source_cards.front: How do U-turn rules differ in residential and business districts?
source_cards.back: U-turns are legal in a residential district when a traffic sign or signal protects you from approaching vehicles, but never in a business district except at an intersection or a provided opening.

source_cards.front: How does passing on the left differ from passing on the right?

source_cards.front: How do you start parallel parking on the right?
source_cards.back: For parallel parking on the right, choose a space about five feet longer than your car, pull up beside the car ahead of it about two or three feet away with rear bumpers lined up, then back slowly with the wheel turned fully right.

source_cards.front: When do you straighten the wheels while parallel parking, and what goes wrong if you don't?
source_cards.back: Once the back of your front seat lines up with the other car's rear bumper, steer smoothly left to straighten; not straightening makes the right rear wheel hit the curb, and over-steering left can bring the right front fender into that car.

source_cards.front: How do you finish parallel parking?
source_cards.back: Finish parallel parking about eighteen inches from the curb, then shift to park in an automatic or to first gear or reverse in a manual, and set the parking brake.

source_cards.front: How far from a fire hydrant must you park?
source_cards.back: Do not park within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant where parallel parking is allowed, or within twenty feet of one where angle parking is allowed.

source_cards.front: How do the hydrant, crosswalk and signal parking distances compare?
source_cards.back: Fire hydrant clearance is fifteen feet for parallel parking but twenty feet for angle parking, and a crosswalk needs twenty feet while a roadside traffic signal needs thirty feet.

source_cards.front: Which way do the tires turn in each hill-parking case?

source_cards.front: Are U-turns generally legal in Nevada, and from which lane?
source_cards.back: U-turns are generally legal on any Nevada road where they can be made safely; signal and make them from the far left lane or the center left-turn lane.

source_cards.back: Never make a U-turn where a curve, hill, rain, fog or anything else keeps you from seeing two hundred feet clearly in each direction.

source_cards.front: What other limits apply to U-turns near hills and in local areas?
source_cards.back: A U-turn is forbidden near a grade where visibility is under five hundred feet in both directions, and local authorities and the state transportation department may ban U-turns at any location they control.

source_cards.front: Why can't you make a U-turn mid-block in a business district?

source_cards.front: May you pass on the left of a driver turning left?
source_cards.back: Never pass on the left of a driver who is making or signalling a left turn.

source_cards.front: When does the slow-left-lane rule not apply?

source_cards.back: Cyclists may not deliberately interfere with motor vehicles, just as motorists may not deliberately interfere with cyclists.

source_cards.back: Never speed up to pass a cyclist just before you turn, and check for cyclists before opening a parked car's door or backing out of a driveway or lot.

source_cards.back: Children and other inexperienced riders may not follow traffic rules, so give them extra care and expect the unexpected, and check both ways for cyclists when turning into an intersection or driveway.

source_cards.back: Clues to a motorcyclist's next move include the rider or passenger turning their head to look back and the rider starting to lean or tilt the motorcycle.

source_cards.front: What can push a motorcycle out of position on the road?
source_cards.back: Strong winds or a rough road surface can push a motorcycle out of its position on the road.

source_cards.front: How should you approach a motorcycle from behind?
source_cards.back: Approaching a motorcycle from behind, begin slowing earlier than you would for a car and keep a generous gap.

source_cards.front: Why must you dim your headlights for a motorcycle?
source_cards.back: Always dim your headlights when approaching a motorcycle, because riders steer by balance and high-beam glare is more dangerous to them than to car or truck drivers.

source_cards.front: How much following distance should you leave behind a motorcycle in rain?
source_cards.back: Leave even more following distance behind a motorcycle when it is raining or the road is slippery.

source_cards.front: What does riding a motorcycle require on a Nevada license?
source_cards.back: Riding a motorcycle requires a special endorsement on a Nevada driver's license.

source_cards.front: How do motorcycles and mopeds differ in licensing and lane rules?
source_cards.back: Motorcycles need a license endorsement, while mopeds, limited in horsepower and to a top speed of thirty miles per hour, must keep to the far right lane in most situations.

source_cards.front: How should drivers treat mopeds compared with motorcycles?
source_cards.back: Drivers around mopeds take the same precautions as around motorcycles, and moped riders share the same rights and duties as other drivers plus extra ones tied to their vehicle's limits.

source_cards.front: What rules must cyclists follow at signals and crosswalks?
source_cards.back: Cyclists must obey all signs and signals, and a cyclist who crosses an intersection in a crosswalk should get off and walk across as a pedestrian.

source_cards.front: Must motorists yield to cyclists at intersections?
source_cards.back: At intersections, motorists must yield to cyclists just as they would to other vehicles and pedestrians.

source_cards.front: What charge can a driver face for any pedestrian collision?
source_cards.back: Drivers must use due care to avoid hitting a pedestrian, and a driver who causes any pedestrian collision, however minor, can face a reckless driving charge.

source_cards.front: Where does a crosswalk exist even if it is not painted?
source_cards.back: A crosswalk exists wherever two streets meet, including a T intersection, whether or not it is painted.

source_cards.front: Whom must you yield to when your light turns green or you turn right?
source_cards.back: When your light turns green, yield to anyone still crossing, and pedestrians have the right-of-way over drivers turning right.

source_cards.front: Which pedestrians in a crosswalk must you yield to?
source_cards.back: Yield, slow or stop for a pedestrian in a crosswalk on your half of the road or the half you are turning into, or one coming so close from the other half as to be in danger.

source_cards.front: When may a vehicle that yielded to a pedestrian move on?
source_cards.back: A vehicle yielding to a pedestrian should wait until the person has crossed into the lanes heading the other way before moving on.

source_cards.front: Where should pedestrians walk when there is no sidewalk?
source_cards.back: Where there is a sidewalk pedestrians should use it, and where there is none they should walk on the side of the road facing oncoming traffic.

source_cards.front: Where should you take extra care around pedestrians?
source_cards.back: Drive with extra care around pedestrians near schools, crosswalks, stop signs, signals and transit stops, especially when children are present.

source_cards.front: What safety habits should pedestrians follow?
source_cards.back: Pedestrians should use crosswalks and obey their signals, not start on a flashing Don't Walk, look left, right and left again, make eye contact with stopping drivers, and at night carry a flashlight and wear reflective gear.

source_cards.front: How close to the crosswalk should you stop for a blind pedestrian?
source_cards.back: When stopping for a blind or visually impaired pedestrian, stop no more than five feet from the crosswalk, since such a pedestrian uses your engine sound as a guide.

source_cards.front: How long should you give a blind pedestrian to decide, and when may you go?
source_cards.back: Give a blind or visually impaired pedestrian time to decide, about three to four seconds; if the person steps back and pulls in the cane, you may go.

source_cards.front: What should you avoid doing around a blind pedestrian?
source_cards.back: Around a blind or visually impaired pedestrian, do not call out directions, do not honk, do not stop in the middle of the crosswalk and do not block the sidewalk.

source_cards.front: What should you do at crosswalks and in a quiet electric vehicle?
source_cards.back: Stop at every crosswalk where pedestrians are waiting, look before any right turn, and be extra alert for blind pedestrians when driving a nearly silent electric vehicle.

source_cards.front: Who causes most crashes between large trucks and cars, and who is hurt most?
source_cards.back: Most crashes between large trucks and smaller cars are caused by the car drivers, and the people in the cars are far more likely to be killed or hurt.

source_cards.front: What is the no-zone around a truck or bus?
source_cards.back: The no-zone is the set of blind spots around a large truck or bus, at its sides, rear and front, where a car effectively disappears from the driver's view.

source_cards.front: Why is the right-side no-zone doubly dangerous?
source_cards.back: The right-side no-zone is doubly dangerous because trucks and buses swing wide when turning right.

source_cards.front: How can you tell whether a truck driver can see you beside the truck?
source_cards.back: Do not linger beside a truck or bus: if you cannot see the driver's face in their side mirror, the driver cannot see you.

source_cards.front: How much more stopping time and distance do large trucks need than cars?
source_cards.back: Large trucks and buses need nearly twice the time and distance cars need to stop, so cutting in front and slowing can get you rear-ended.

source_cards.front: When may you move back in front of a truck you have passed?
source_cards.back: After passing a truck or bus, wait until its whole front shows in your rearview mirror before moving into its lane, and then do not slow down.

source_cards.front: Why should you never tailgate a truck or bus?
source_cards.back: Do not tailgate a truck or bus: its driver cannot see you directly behind, you cannot see the road beyond it, and a sudden stop leaves you nowhere to go.

source_cards.front: How do the dangers of the front and rear no-zones differ?
source_cards.back: In the front no-zone the danger is cutting in too soon and slowing, which can get you rear-ended, while in the rear no-zone the danger is tailgating, where neither driver can see the other's situation.

source_cards.front: Why must you never pass behind a truck that is backing up?

source_cards.front: Why should you never squeeze between a turning truck and the curb?
source_cards.back: Trucks and buses may swing wide left to make a right turn, or wide right to make a left turn, so never try to squeeze between one and the curb.

source_cards.back: In Nevada, no one under eighteen may ride in a pickup bed or on a flatbed truck on a paved highway, except in a parade authorized by a local authority or while farming or ranching.
